info.title: Hanzo Cloud API
info.description: Package task is Hanzo Task: boards, the work items on them, and the filters that make a board.

get.summary: Returns a board's issues — work items with their column, priority, assignee, labels and schedule.
get.description:
Returns a board's issues — work items with their column, priority,
assignee, labels and schedule.

WHICH board is a filter, not an address. Bound to a repository (the key from
the path) it is that project's board; left unbound it is the org's whole
board; narrowed by label it is a board smaller than any repository — which is
the only way an app that lives as a directory inside a shared repository can
have one. Every combination is the same rows through the same projection, so
no two boards can disagree about what a column means.

The column is a LABEL on the forge, so the board and the forge web UI are the
same object seen twice: relabelling in either moves the card in both. A closed
issue reads as done whatever its labels say.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description:
Key is the project whose issues to list, from the path. EMPTY means every
project in the org — the global board. It is a filter like the rest of
this struct rather than an address, which is what lets one op answer both
"this board" and "all the work" without a second surface disagreeing with
the first about what a column is.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description:
Status keeps only issues in that board column: backlog, todo, in_progress,
done or canceled. An unknown value is refused with 400.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description:
Kind keeps only work items of that shape: issue, pr or epic. An unknown
value is refused with 400.

parameters.name: repo
parameters.description: Repo keeps only issues bound to that git repository.

parameters.name: label
parameters.description:
Label keeps only issues carrying that label, compared case-insensitively.

This is how a board narrows to something SMALLER than a repository — the
one mechanism for it. An estate whose apps are directories inside one
repository (hanzoai/cloud carries ~140 of them) has no repository per app
to address, so the app is a label: `label=app/meet` is the meet board.
Nothing is provisioned to make one exist; a board is the query.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description:
Source keeps only issues opened from that surface: team, git, crm,
helpdesk, cms or agent. An unknown value is refused with 400.

parameters.name: scheduled
parameters.description:
Scheduled keeps only issues that carry a date — a start, a due date or
both. This is the timeline's slice of the board: pass scheduled=true to
get exactly the rows a gantt has somewhere to draw, instead of fetching
every issue and discarding the undated ones client-side.

get.description:
Summarises one channel's work.

The channel is opaque here and is deliberately not resolved: this package cannot
say whether a channel exists — apps/team owns that document — so an unknown channel
answers an EMPTY board rather than a 404. That is the honest answer and the
useful one: a channel that has never had an item filed in it and a channel id
that was mistyped both have no work, and inventing a distinction would require
this surface to hold a second copy of the channel list (HIP-0523 §2 forbids it,
and it would drift the first time a channel was renamed).

Tenancy is the validated principal's org and nothing else, so a caller cannot
read another tenant's channel by naming its channel.

parameters.name: channel
parameters.description:
Channel is the channel, spelled "<space>_<channel>" — the same value
GET /v1/meet/call answers with, so a channel's call and its work name the
channel identically. From the path.

get.summary: Answers across every project in the org.
get.description:
Answers across every project in the org.

The org comes from the validated principal and never from the request: a
caller able to name the org could read another tenant's backlog, and a search
is exactly the shape that would quietly return it.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description:
Q matches an issue's title or description. A word from the issue, which is
what someone remembers — not its number, which is what they are looking up.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description:
Project narrows to one team key; "" searches every project in the org,
which is the point of this op.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Status keeps one board column: backlog, todo, in_progress, done, canceled.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Kind keeps one shape: issue, pr, epic.

parameters.name: repo
parameters.description: Repo keeps issues bound to one git repository.

parameters.name: channel
parameters.description:
Channel keeps issues bound to one collaboration channel, spelled
"<space>_<channel>" — the exact value GET /v1/meet/call answers with, so a
channel's call and its task list name the channel the same way. This is the
read a channel view runs to draw its own list; it spans every board of the
org, because the work a channel is about is not confined to one board.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description:
Source keeps one origin: team, git, crm, helpdesk, cms, agent. "git" is
how you ask for the mirrored GitHub issues specifically.

parameters.name: assignee
parameters.description: Assignee keeps issues held by one person. Pass "me" for yourself.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description:
Limit caps the answer; 0 means the default, and anything above the ceiling
is clamped rather than refused — a search that errors on being too broad
teaches people to guess.

get.summary: Returns the boards of your org — the places your work actually is.
get.description:
Returns the boards of your org — the places your work actually
is. The key addresses the board's issues.

A BOARD IS A PLACE WORK IS, not an object somebody provisioned. So the list is
assembled from the work itself: the repositories your org has filed issues on,
plus the boards the index holds. A repository with nothing on it is not in the
list and is still perfectly addressable — GET /projects/<name> reads it and a
create files into it — so nothing is lost by leaving it out.

Measured, which is why: reading the forge's whole repository inventory put 745
boards here, of which all but a handful were vendored forks and mirrors
(.github, .profile, DOMPurify, BoatAttack) that will never carry this org's
work. A list that long is not a list — the estate's real roadmap was in it
somewhere and no one could see it.

The forge half is the FORGE's answer for your own account, so two people in
one org can legitimately see different boards.

post.summary: Refused — a board is a repository on the forge
post.description:
Answers 405. A task board IS a repository on this deployment's forge, so creating, renaming and deleting one is a FORGE operation carried out with FORGE permissions.

Offering it here would put a second endpoint on the same object, guarded by this surface instead of by the forge — a weaker guard on the same thing. So the route exists and refuses, rather than 404ing: "not this service's job" and "no such thing" are different facts, and the body names the forge so a caller knows where the job IS done.

What this surface DOES own is the work on a board: list the boards you can see, read and file their issues, move a card between columns, and read the schedule a milestone is. Those are the routes beside this one.

delete.description:

Offering it here would put a second endpoint on the same object, guarded by this surface instead of by the forge — a weaker guard on the same thing. So the route exists and refuses, rather than 404ing: "not this service's job" and "no such thing" are different facts, and the body names the forge so a caller knows where the job IS done.

What this surface DOES own is the work on a board: list the boards you can see, read and file their issues, move a card between columns, and read the schedule a milestone is. Those are the routes beside this one.

get.summary: Returns one board of your org by its key — the repository name.
get.description:
Returns one board of your org by its key — the repository name.
404 when your org has no repository under that key, or when your own forge
account cannot see it.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description:
Key is the project's org-unique handle: 2-8 uppercase alphanumerics starting
with a letter ("ENG", "OPS2"). Matched case-insensitively.

patch.summary: Refused — a board is a repository on the forge
patch.description:

post.summary: Opens a work item on the board, filed as YOU, where the repository lives: an issue on the deployment's forge, or on GitHub for a repository the forge mirrors from there or does not hold at all.
post.description:
Opens a work item on the board, filed as YOU, where the
repository lives: an issue on the deployment's forge, or on GitHub for a
repository the forge mirrors from there or does not hold at all. Answers 201
with the card: its `number`, its `id`, and the issue's address as `url`. A
create that cannot say what it made answers 502, never an empty 2xx.

The column and priority are written as LABELS, which is what makes the card
and the issue the same object: someone relabelling in the web UI has moved
your card.

Asked for in a chat thread, the issue is bound to that thread, and what
happens to it on GitHub is said there.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description:
Key is the board — the repository name, from the path. `owner/name`, or
`github.com/owner/name`, names a repository on GitHub that no board on the
forge stands for.

get.summary: Returns ONE work item in full — its description included.
get.description:
Returns ONE work item in full — its description included.

The list reads answer a board, and a board is a summary: the description is
where the actual content of a work item lives — what an issue asks for, what
an epic's acceptance criteria are — and no read on this surface returned it.
The address is the one PATCH already accepts, so an item you can move is now
an item you can read.

It reads the forge directly rather than filtering the org fan-out, then falls
back to the index for a board the forge has never heard of — the same order,
and the same reason, as GetProject: a row is one kind of thing however it came
to exist, so a caller does not have to know which store it is in to fetch it.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key is the board — the repository name, or an index board's key.

parameters.name: num
parameters.description: Num is the issue's number on that board.

patch.summary: Edits a work item — rename it, rewrite it, move it to another column, re-prioritise it, hand it to somebody, or comment on it.
patch.description:
Edits a work item — rename it, rewrite it, move it to another
column, re-prioritise it, hand it to somebody, or comment on it. Absent fields
are left alone. An issue on GitHub is edited there.

MOVING A CARD IS A RELABEL. The column lives in the forge's label set, so the
move replaces that set rather than writing a status column here that a
forge-side change could contradict. Moving to `done` also CLOSES the issue,
because a done card and an open issue are a contradiction.

Assigning it to `agent` hands it to the coding agent: see `assignee`.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key is the board — the repository name, from the path.

parameters.name: num
parameters.description: Num is the issue number on that repository, from the path.

post.summary: Takes an issue: it becomes yours and it moves to in_progress.
post.description:
Takes an issue: it becomes yours and it moves to in_progress.

The holder is the CALLER, never an argument. "Assign this to someone else" is
a different act with different authority, and it already exists as a PATCH;
conflating them would let anyone hand work to anyone by naming them.

Claiming something already held by someone else is refused rather than
silently taken — two agents on one issue is the failure this prevents, and a
claim that quietly wins a race is worse than one that says no.

get.summary: Is one issue's conversation, oldest first, read as the caller.
get.description:
Is one issue's conversation, oldest first, read as the caller.
An issue that lives on GitHub names its home and is read there.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key is the board — the repository name, or an index board's key.

parameters.name: num
parameters.description: Num is the issue's number on that board.

code.description: A stable token a client can branch on, when the refusal names one.

detail.description: What was refused, for a person to read.

channel.description:
Channel is the conversation inside that workspace, and it is what decides whether
there is an address at all. Empty is the ordinary case: a caller of
/v1/agent/coding holds a session id and reads the stream instead.

provider.description:
Provider is the transport the conversation is on — slack, discord,
telegram, teams — and it is what decides who can carry the text at all. An
address without it names a channel in no particular workspace.

thread.description:
Thread narrows the address to one thread inside the channel — on Slack the
parent message's ts, the same value a reply carries as thread_ts. Empty
puts the text at the top level of the channel.

turn.description:
Turn is the turn that renders a run started here: the session whose one
message the run's progress and its outcome are shown in. A run with a Turn
posts nothing of its own — one question, one message. The dispatcher writes
it (apps/agents/replyto.go); a model never does.

user.description:
User is the platform's id for the person the conversation is with — whose
run it is. A run's buttons name them to anyone else who presses one; it is
never what decides who may (that is the chat identity).

createdAt.description:
CreatedAt is when the board was created, in unix seconds. 0 on a forge board
for the same reason Description is absent.

description.description:
Description is whatever an index board was created with. Absent on a forge
board: this projection takes the repository's name and nothing else about the
repository.

id.description:
ID is the board's opaque handle, and it is NOT how you address it — Key is.
Its shape says which source answered: a forge board's is the repository's
full name ("hanzoai/cloud"), an index board's a minted "prj_" id.

key.description:
Key addresses the board everywhere else — /v1/task/projects/<key>/issues —
and prefixes every issue identifier on it. An index board's key is 2-8
uppercase alphanumerics starting with a letter ("ENG", "OPS2") and is matched
case-insensitively; a forge board's is the repository name as the forge
spells it.

name.description:
Name is the board's display name. For a forge board it is the repository
name, so it equals Key; an index board carries its own.

org.description:
Org is the IAM org the board belongs to, taken from the validated principal
and never from the request. Every board a caller can see is in it.

updatedAt.description:
UpdatedAt is when the board record last changed, in unix seconds — the BOARD,
not the work on it, so filing an issue does not move it. 0 on a forge board.

channel.description: Channel is the channel these counts are for, echoed back as it was resolved.

open.description:
Open is how many items are still work: everything whose status does not
end it. It is the number a channel header shows.

status.description:
Status is the count per board column, carrying EVERY column this surface
knows — an empty column reads 0 rather than being absent, so a caller can
render the board without inventing the vocabulary. The keys are the same
closed set every other operation here validates against.

total.description:
Total is every item bound to this channel, settled ones included, so Total
minus Open is what the channel has finished.

updated.description:
Updated is when anything in this channel's work last moved, in unix seconds.
ABSENT when the channel has no work at all: zero would read as the epoch, and
a channel nobody has filed anything in has no last activity rather than an
infinitely old one. Total is 0 in exactly that case.

author.description: Author is who wrote it: their name, else their forge login.

body.description: Body is what was written, as markdown.

createdAt.description: CreatedAt is when it was written, RFC 3339.

id.description: ID is the forge's id for the comment.

data.description: Data is the conversation. Empty is an empty array, never null.

home.description:
Home is the GitHub repository (owner/name) the issue lives on when its board
mirrors one; its conversation is read there, and Data is then empty.

assignee.description:
Assignee hands the work to somebody — a person or an agent, by the name
they are known by on the forge. "" TAKES IT OFF whoever holds it, which is
why this is a pointer: absent leaves the holder alone.

It is the other half of `claim`, which that handler already named: a claim
takes work for the CALLER and refuses to name anyone else, because giving
work away is a different act with different authority. This is that act,
and until it existed a board could only be worked by whoever clicked
first — an agent could never be given anything.

`me` is you, by the GitHub account IAM links to you (or your forge login).
`agent` hands the issue to the coding agent: it is labelled `agent`, and a
coding run starts on its repository with the issue as the task, narrating
in the thread the hand-off was asked in; its pull request closes the issue.
Labelling an issue `agent` on GitHub does the same.

comment.description:
Comment is posted on the issue, after every other change — what a person in
the issue's thread wants said on it.

key.description: Key is the board — the repository name, from the path.

num.description: Num is the issue number on that repository, from the path.

reply.description:
Reply is the conversation the edit was asked for in, written by a chat turn
and never chosen (see newIssue). An issue bound to no thread is bound to
this one, and a run the edit starts narrates here.

status.description: Status moves the card to another column.

assignee.description:
Assignee is who holds the work. EMPTY MEANS UNHELD, which is what makes the
issue claimable: claiming one already held by someone else is refused with
409 rather than quietly taken.

channel.description:
Channel is the collaboration channel the issue belongs to, spelled
"<space>_<channel>" — empty when it is not channel-bound, which is most of
them. It is here so an org-wide search says which channel each item came
from without a second read.

kind.description: Kind is what the row IS: issue, pr or epic.

number.description:
Number is the issue's number on that board, from 1 and monotonic there.
Unique per board, never across the org — so it addresses an issue only
together with Project.

priority.description:
Priority is urgent, high, medium, low or none. Never empty — an unset
priority is the value "none".

project.description:
Project is the board key the issue is on. It and Number are the issue's
address in every other route on this surface, which is why a hit carries it.

repo.description:
Repo is the git repository the issue is bound to, empty when it is not
repo-bound.

source.description:
Source is which surface opened it: team, git, crm, helpdesk, cms or agent.
"git" is how the mirrored forge and GitHub rows are spelled.

status.description:
Status is the board column: backlog, todo, in_progress, done or canceled.
Claiming moves backlog and todo to in_progress and leaves the other three
where they are.

title.description:
Title is the issue's one-line summary — what the q filter matched, along with
the description.

url.description:
URL is the row's external anchor — its extRef — which is a link only when the
feeder sent one. A mirrored GitHub issue carries "github:owner/repo#123" and
an agent's PR row carries the pushed branch. Empty for a row opened here.

count.description:
Count is how many rows Issues carries — the size of THIS answer after the
cap, not how many issues matched. A count equal to the limit means there are
probably more; there is no total and no cursor.

issues.description:
Issues are the matching rows grouped by status and oldest-first within a
group, capped by the search's limit (50 by default, 200 at most). The cap is
applied to that order, so a broad search returns the head of it rather than a
sample.

assignee.description:
Assignee is who holds the work — an IAM username, or the login of the FIRST
assignee when a forge issue has several. Absent when nobody holds it, which
is exactly the state a claim needs.

createdAt.description:
CreatedAt is when the item was opened, in unix seconds. 0 when the source
gave no parseable timestamp.

description.description: Description is the body, markdown as its author wrote it. Absent when empty.

dueAt.description:
DueAt is when the work is due, in unix seconds; absent means no due date. A
forge row takes it from its MILESTONE's due date, since a forge issue has no
deadline of its own. Never before StartAt, and never past 2200-01-01.

extRef.description:
ExtRef anchors the item to something outside the task — a mirrored issue
("github:owner/repo#123"), a pushed PR branch, or a record on another plane.
It is the idempotency key the mirror upsert matches on. Absent when the item
has no external origin.

id.description:
ID is the work item's opaque handle, and it is NOT how you address it —
ProjectKey plus Number is. Its shape says which source answered: a forge
issue's is the forge's own numeric id in decimal, an index row's a minted
"issue_" id.

identifier.description:
Identifier is the human handle, "<key>#<number>" — the board and the number
on it, joined. ONE spelling whichever source answered, because a list where
forge rows read cli#1 and index rows read OPS-3 is two products in one list.

kind.description:
Kind is what the item IS: issue, pr or epic. Set once at create and never
changed, so a row does not migrate between surfaces. Deliberately not "task"
— that word is the async plane (contract.go).

labels.description:
Labels are the item's remaining tags, with the status and priority labels
lifted OUT — a column that stayed here would render twice, once as the card's
column and once as a chip on the card. Always present; empty is [].

number.description:
Number is the item's number ON ITS BOARD, from 1 and monotonic there — the
forge's own issue number for a forge row, allocated inside the create
transaction for an index row so it cannot race. Unique per board, never
across the org.

priority.description:
Priority is urgent, high, medium, low or none. Also a label on a forge row.
Never empty: "none" when nothing names one, so callers compare a value rather
than test for absence.

projectKey.description:
ProjectKey is the board this item is on: the repository name for a forge
issue, the index board's key otherwise. With Number it is the item's address
in every other route.

repo.description:
Repo is the git repository the item is bound to, so a repository's Issues and
PRs tabs are filters over this one table. Absent when the item is not
repo-bound.

source.description:
Source is which surface OPENED it: team, git, crm, helpdesk, cms or agent.
Also set once. It is the ORIGIN, not the subject — source=helpdesk is an
engineering issue opened from a support escalation, not a support ticket.

startAt.description:
StartAt is when the work starts, in unix seconds; absent means unscheduled.
A forge row takes it from when the issue was opened, but only once the issue
has a due date — an interval needs both ends.

status.description:
Status is the board column: backlog, todo, in_progress, done or canceled, and
nothing else. On a forge row it is read off a LABEL, so relabelling in the
forge web UI moves the card here and vice versa — and a CLOSED forge issue
reads done whatever its labels say. Never empty: "backlog" when nothing names
a column.

title.description: Title is the item's one-line summary.

updatedAt.description: UpdatedAt is when it last changed, in unix seconds.

url.description:
URL is where a person reads the item: its page on the forge or on GitHub.
Absent for an index row, which has no page of its own.

key.description:
Key is the board — the repository name, from the path. `owner/name`, or
`github.com/owner/name`, names a repository on GitHub that no board on the
forge stands for.

priority.description: Priority is one of none, urgent, high, medium or low.

reply.description:
Reply is the conversation the issue was asked for in. A chat turn writes
its own thread here, over anything else (apps/agents replyto.go); it is not
a value to choose. The issue is bound to it, and what happens to the issue
next — comments, closing, who holds it, a pull request that closes it — is
said there.

status.description:
Status is the board column to open into: backlog, todo, in_progress, done
or canceled. Empty opens into backlog.

title.description:
Title is the one line the card is read by on the board. Blank or whitespace
is refused — an untitled card cannot be told apart from any other.

bearer.description: The caller's credential, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. It is either an access token minted by Hanzo IAM or an API key (pk-/sk-). X-Authorization, and HTTP Basic carrying the token as the password, are accepted spellings of the same header for clients that cannot set Authorization; a browser presents the session cookie instead. Every operation requires it unless it says `security: []`.
